newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada oil firms eyeing North Sea acquisitions.
newsitem.headline: Canada oil firms eyeing North Sea acquisitions.

text.p: Canadian oil and gas companies, long content to gain gradual international exposure through exploration, are expected increasingly to be eyeing overseas acquisitions, many in the North Sea.

Gulf Canada Resources Ltd in December made waves Britain's energy sector with its 432 million pound (US$730 million) hostile bid for Clyde Petroleum Plc, which has production in the North Sea, Australia and Indonesia.
Gulf, now locked in a vexed debate over methods used by Clyde to value its operations, had long coveted the North Sea as a major new core production area.
The takeover play followed a friendly deal completed early last year in which Talisman Energy Inc absorbed Goal Petroleum, a firm with production complementing Talisman's own North Sea operations.

"Can I see a scenario where we see more Canadian producers acquiring international production, be it corporate or assets? Absolutely -- I think we'll continue to see that," said Matt Janisch, analyst at Nesbitt Burns in Calgary.

The oil and gas evolution in the North Sea is currently at a similar point to that in western Canada about four years ago, when small and medium-size independents scooped up production jettisoned by the majors, Janisch said.

In the early 1990s, reserves in Alberta, British Columbia and Saskatchewan that were deemed too small to impact industry behemoths became major purchases and and new core areas for hundreds of smaller firms.
"There's a view that Canadian producers can do that by going in and buying assets or companies in the North Sea," said Janisch.
The attraction to the North Sea's proven reserves and high per-barrel netbacks compared to Canada show companies are searching for steady cash flow instead of major new oil finds.

"There's still potential in the North Sea, but it's a different type of potential," he said. "It's optimization and smaller-field stepout (drilling). But if you look at, say West Africa, people are still looking for the big hit."

Prominent Canadian operators in the North Sea include Talisman, Ranger Oil Ltd and Canadian Occidental Petroleum Ltd. Of those, Talisman and Ranger in 1996 increased their holdings with asset acquisitions and swaps.

Ranger vice-president John Faulds noted advantages for firms which have been active in the region for several years because of their operating expertise and inventories of assets on which to build or to swap.

"We have an acreage position, we've got some chips we can trade," Faulds said, adding that operating costs have dropped dramatically thanks to new technologies like extended reach drilling and floating production systems.
However, the Gulf-Clyde struggle has spotlighted potential pitfalls in trying to ink deals in unfamiliar jurisdications.
